newsitem.title: USA: Dow soars above 6,900 on strong dollar; bonds unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Dow soars above 6,900 on strong dollar; bonds unchanged.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average soared above the 6,900-point mark for the first time in heavy trading Wednesday, propelled by a strong dollar and powerful mutual fund inflows.
Bonds were little changed after a disappointing 10-year Treasury auction.
The steep gains brought the world's most closely-watched blue-chip index near the 7,000 milestone. The Standard & Poor's composite index set a new high, and the Nasdaq index rose more than 2 percent.
The Dow ended up 103.52 points, or 1.51 percent, at a record 6,961.63, breezing through the old high of 6,883.90 set on Jan. 21.
In the broader market, advancing issues swamped declines 1,757 to 758 on heavy volume of 563 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The sweeping rally, helped by a strong dollar and powerful mutual fund inflows, left few sectors behind. Technology, financial, energy, gold mining and transportation shares all surged.

Analysts said the sudden burst of investors' confidence was rooted in the technology sector, which got a critical boost when semiconductor equipment maker Applied Materials Inc. reported surprisingly strong quarterly profits late Tuesday. Applied Materials stock surged $7 to $52.125.
The earnings triggered a sharp technology rally that quickly spread to the broader market.
"The Applied Materials results definitely helped," said Bill Meehan, an analyst at Prudential Securities.

"If you step back and look, we spent a good deal of January ratcheting up interest rates and that didn't break the market," he said. "Then we got some technology disappointments and even in the face of those we're having a strong rebound."
The renewed appetite for stocks came amid fresh reports that investors were pouring more cash into U.S. stock mutual funds.

The Investment Company Institute, a trade group, said net cash flows into such funds nearly doubled in January to $24 billion from $12.22 billion in December, but were still not as high as the record $28.9 billion in January 1996.

Also lending support was the dollar, which worked its way still higher, gaining ground against both the German mark and the Japanese yen. The dollar ended at 1.6871 marks, up from 1.6773 late Tuesday, and at 124.25 yen, up from 123.28.

The dollar hit a 34-month peak against the German mark and approached a four-year high against the Japanese yen in early trading, supported by a New York Times article citing American exporters' relative comfort with an extended rally that has powered the U.S. currency higher.
In the bond market, the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged, leaving the yield at 6.71 percent.
Frozen concentrated orange juice prices fell sharply after the U.S. Agriculture Department reported Florida's orange crop survived a winter freeze in good shape.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, March frozen concentrated orange juice closed down 5.35 cents to 74.55 cents a pound after earlier falling to a contract low of 72.50 cents.
Soybean prices bounded higher after the Agriculture Department reported smaller-than-expected stocks of both before this year's harvests.
At the Chicago Board of Trade March soybeans closed up 14-1/2 cents at $7.64-1/4 per bushel after peaking at $7.65-1/2 per bushel, the highest since Oct. 2 when that contract touched $7.75.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index of leading shares finished unchanged at 4,304.3. In Tokyo, key Nikkei 225 average rose 228.79 points to end at 18,409.96.
